place.en: Black Pine Ridge · the stream at the valley mouth

setup.zh: 那头鹿还在谷口的溪边喝水：三百步，东北，顺风。爹的手在抖，把爷爷的弓递给了你。
setup.en: The deer is still drinking at the stream by the valley mouth: three hundred paces, northeast, downwind. Father's hands shake; he gives you grandfather's bow.

recap.zh: 你拉开爷爷的弓射中了那头雄鹿；银月撑着说完指路的话，晕了过去。
recap.en: You drew grandfather's bow and brought down the stag; Yinyue held on long enough to guide the shot, and fainted.

zh: 一头雄鹿低头饮水，角如枯枝。
en: A stag drinks, antlers like dead branches.
The bow is heavier than you thought.

story.zh:
一行人正要下山，银月忽然在小满耳边开了口。

⟪「那头鹿。」⟫

她的声音比方才更小了，小得像一根线，一口气倒像要分成三口来说：「谷口……溪边……在喝水。三百步，东北，顺风。」

小满脚下一顿，低声道：「你怎么知道？」

「本王是妖王。」

「妖王也管打猎？」

她停了一停，才道：「……本王欠你一张饼。先还个利息。」

小满心里一跳。三百步，东北，溪边——昨儿晌午，他爹在山涧边上摸着的那个蹄印，比巴掌还宽，蹄印便是往东北去的。爷儿俩追了它一个时辰，追进了黑松岭，追得天塌了下来，儿子追下了崖，老子的膝盖罢了工，它却在溪边喝水。小满心想，这头鹿大约是天底下最沉得住气的一头鹿了。

他拉了拉他爹的袖子，朝东北指了一指，道：「爹。鹿。」

他爹要去，老周拦他：「你那腿——」他爹道：「腿不行。」顿了一顿，又道：「还有孩子的腿。」这句话，他前一日早上跟小满他娘也说过一回，一个字都不差，小满听着，便觉得这句话大概是他家的家训。老周叹了口气，叫那两个后生扛着门板在坡上等着，他自己把烟袋往腰里一别，跟了上来。

三人摸过去。从那道坡往东北，是一道缓缓的斜坡，坡上长满了半人高的枯草，草底下是松软的腐叶，踩上去没有声息。小满走在最前头，他爹跟在后头，老周跟在最后头。老周的脚步很重，踩断了一根枯枝，「咔嚓」一声，小满他爹回头瞪了他一眼，老周便把两只鞋脱了，拎在手里，光着脚走。走满三百步，只听得水声潺潺，小满伏在一丛灌木后面，拨开枝叶往外一看，果然是一道溪，溪边一头雄鹿正低着头喝水。

小满这辈子没见过那样的鹿。它比他家那扇门还高，身上的毛是赭红的，油光水滑，太阳底下一照，亮得像一块缎子。它头上那对角，像一丛冬天的枯树枝，枝枝杈杈，数也数不清，比他爹这辈子见过的所有鹿都大。它喝一口水，便抬起头来，竖着两只耳朵往四下里听一听，又低下头去喝一口。水珠子从它下巴上一滴一滴往下掉，掉进溪里，叮咚叮咚的。

他爹伏在他身边，看了那头鹿一眼，呼吸便粗了。他解下背上的弓，搭上了箭，要站起来——却站不起来。他那条左腿在坡上趴了一夜，这时候又冷又僵，像一根冻透了的柴火，他撑着地使了两回劲，膝盖只是「咯」地响了一声，身子却一寸也没抬起来。他咬着牙，想换个法子，跪着射——左膝一沾地，整张脸便白了，白得像溪边那几块石头。

那头鹿又抬起头来，竖着耳朵听。风从它那边吹过来，它闻不见人，可它听得见，老周的喘气声太响了。

小满低声道：「爹。我来。」

他爹看着他。看了很久很久，久到那头鹿又低下头去喝了两口水。然后他把爷爷的弓，递给了儿子。

那弓比小满想的沉得多。

弓弦是牛筋拧的，勒进手指头里，像勒进了一块豆腐。拉到一半，胳膊便开始打颤，颤得那支箭在弓背上一跳一跳的，箭头对着那头鹿，一会儿对着它的脖子，一会儿对着它的屁股，一会儿又对着它头上那丛枯树枝，好像拿不定主意，到底该射它哪儿。他又往后拉了一寸，左手腕里「喀」的一声轻响，也不知是骨头响，还是心里响，只觉得一股酸疼从手腕一直窜到了肩膀。

他爹在身后轻声道：「先看风。」

小满看风。溪边的芦草一阵往这边倒，一阵又直起来。风是一阵一阵的。他爹说过，风一阵一阵的，便等它歇一口气。他等着。胳膊在抖，手腕在疼，那头鹿喝饱了水，正在溪边的石头上蹭它的角，蹭得「咯吱咯吱」响，随时都要走。他还是等着。风刮过来，芦草一齐伏倒；风过去了，芦草晃了两晃，慢慢地直起来——

便在这时，银月在他耳边道：⟪「往左偏半寸。」⟫
story.en:
They were just starting down when Yinyue spoke in Xiaoman's ear.

⟪"The deer."⟫

Her voice was smaller than before, thin as a thread, as though one breath had to be split into three: "By the valley mouth… the stream… drinking. Three hundred paces, northeast, downwind."

Xiaoman missed a step. Low: "How do you know?"

"This king is a demon king."

"Demon kings do hunting too?"

She paused before she said: "…This king owes you a flatbread. Here's some interest first."

Xiaoman's heart jumped. Three hundred paces, northeast, by the stream — yesterday noon, the hoofprint his father had felt by the stream, wider than a palm, had led northeast. Father and son had chased it an hour, chased it into Black Pine Ridge, chased it till the sky fell in, the son off a cliff and the father's knee on strike — and it was drinking at the stream. Xiaoman thought this was probably the coolest-headed deer under heaven.

He tugged his father's sleeve and pointed northeast. "Dad. Deer."

His father meant to go; Old Zhou tried to stop him: "That leg of yours —" His father said, "The leg's no good." A pause. "There's the boy's legs too." He'd said that same sentence to Xiaoman's mother the morning before, word for word; Xiaoman thought it was probably the family motto. Old Zhou sighed, told the two young men to wait on the slope with the door-plank, tucked his pipe into his belt, and followed.

The three of them crept over. Northeast of the slope ran a gentle incline thick with dead grass half a man high, soft leaf-mould underneath, soundless underfoot. Xiaoman went first, his father behind, Old Zhou last. Old Zhou's tread was heavy; he snapped a dead twig — *crack* — and Xiaoman's father turned and glared at him, so Old Zhou took off both shoes and carried them, walking barefoot. After three hundred paces there was the sound of running water; Xiaoman lay behind a bush and parted the leaves: a stream, and by it a stag with its head down, drinking.

Xiaoman had never seen a deer like it. It stood taller than the door at home, its coat russet, glossy, gleaming like satin in the sun. The antlers on its head were like a thicket of winter branches, fork on fork, past counting — bigger than any deer his father had seen in his life. It drank a mouthful, raised its head, ears up, listening all round, lowered its head and drank again. Drops fell from its chin one by one into the stream, *ding-dong, ding-dong*.

His father lay beside him, took one look at the deer, and his breath came heavy. He unslung the bow, nocked an arrow, and went to stand — and couldn't. His left leg, after a night lying on the slope, was cold and stiff as a frozen log; he pushed off the ground twice, and the knee only gave a *clack*, and his body didn't rise an inch. He set his teeth and tried another way — to shoot kneeling; the moment his left knee touched the ground his whole face went white, white as the stones by the stream.

The deer raised its head again, ears up. The wind blew from its side; it couldn't smell them, but it could hear, and Old Zhou was breathing too loud.

Xiaoman said low: "Dad. Let me."

His father looked at him. Looked a long, long time, so long the deer lowered its head and drank twice more. Then he handed his son the grandfather's bow.

The bow was much heavier than Xiaoman had imagined.

The string was twisted sinew; it cut into his fingers as into tofu. Halfway drawn his arm began to shake, shaking the arrow on the bow so that the head pointed now at the deer's neck, now at its rump, now at the thicket of winter branches on its head, as if it couldn't make up its mind where to shoot. He drew another inch, and something in his left wrist went *click* — bone or heart, he couldn't tell — and a sour ache shot from wrist to shoulder.

His father said softly behind him: "Read the wind first."

Xiaoman read the wind. The reeds by the stream bent this way in gusts, then straightened again. The wind was gusting. His father had said: when the wind comes in gusts, wait for it to catch its breath. He waited. His arm shook, his wrist ached; the deer had drunk its fill and was rubbing its antlers on a rock by the stream, *creak, creak*, ready to go at any moment. He still waited. A gust came, and the reeds all bowed; the gust passed, and the reeds swayed twice and slowly began to straighten —

Just then Yinyue said in his ear: ⟪"Half an inch to the left."⟫

label.en: Half an inch to the left

exits.means: aims a little left for the wind, as told, and shoots

story.zh:
她的声音很轻，很累，像是从很远很远的地方飘过来的。小满往左偏了半寸。

芦草将直未直。他手指一松。

那箭已离弦而去，「嗖」的一声，他还没瞧清它飞到了哪里，只觉得肩膀上一轻。那只小银狐从他脖子上滑了下来，软软地往下掉。他扔了弓，一把把它接住了——它闭着眼睛，身子凉得像一块冰，比昨儿夜里发烧的时候还要吓人。昨儿夜里它是烫的，烫的至少还是活的；这时候它是凉的，凉得像溪里的石头。小满慌了，把它往怀里一塞，贴着胸口捂着，隔着那件补丁摞补丁的单衣，觉出它很慢、很慢地，还在喘气。

他张了张嘴。他想说「谢了」，或者「谢谢你」，或者别的什么，总之是一句带「谢」字的话。那句话已经到了舌头尖上，可它闭着眼睛，听不见了。

溪边那头鹿轰然倒下。那箭正中它的脖子，不偏不倚。

他爹一瘸一拐地跑过去，那条腿方才还站不起来，这时候不知哪来的力气，跑得比老周还快。他扑通一声跪在鹿旁边——膝盖也顾不得了——伸手去摸那对角，摸了一下，又摸了一下，然后回过头来看儿子，笑得像个孩子。

小满也笑。可他的手一直按在胸口上，没敢松开。

老周跑到溪边，瞧瞧那头鹿，又瞧瞧那支箭，又瞧瞧小满，咂了咂嘴，道：「一箭？」小满他爹道：「一箭。」老周道：「他射的？」他爹道：「他射的。」老周道：「他才十二。」他爹道：「嗯。」老周瞧着他，看了半天，道：「你十二岁的时候，还没摸过这张弓。」他爹道：「我十四才摸。我爹也是十四。」他顿了一顿，低下头去，拿手掌一下一下地摸着那头鹿的脖子，又道：「他十二。」

他没有再说别的。可他说那三个字的时候，那个腔调，和他跟马三说「三爷」的腔调，是不一样的。

到得村口，已是傍晚。

一个是小满他娘。她站在老槐树底下，两只手拢在袖子里，一动不动，像是站了很久。后来小满才知道，她从前一日天黑一直站到这一日傍晚，一整夜，一整天，中间只回过一趟家，是去给灶里添了一把火——她说，万一人回来了，灶是凉的，那可不行。

另一个是阿禾。阿禾站在她旁边，站得很是古怪：两只脚的脚尖，齐齐地抵在老槐树的树根上，一寸也不肯往外挪，身子却往前探着，探得老长，脖子伸得像一只等食的鹅。小满起先不明白她为什么这样站，后来想起来了——她娘不让她出村口，老槐树就是村口。她一只脚也没出去，脖子却已经出去了。

他娘却不嚷。她从老槐树底下走过来，走得不快，也不慢，走到儿子跟前，停下了。她先看他的脸，看了一会儿；又看他的手，看了一会儿；最后看他那只肿着的左手腕。那手腕上缠着的，是他昨儿夜里给狐狸擦伤口剩下的半片衣摆，缠得歪歪扭扭，早给泥水泡成了一条烂布。

他娘一句话也没说，把那条烂布解了下来，从自己衣襟底下撕下一条干净的布，一圈一圈，重新给他缠上。她缠得极慢，极仔细，缠一圈，抻一抻，再缠一圈，缠到最后，打了一个结，那个结打得方方正正，跟她补衣裳打的结一模一样。缠完了，她的手在他手腕上停了一停。

然后她转过身去，看小满他爹。他爹抬着门板的后头，脸上的泥还没洗，一双眼睛红得像兔子。两个人对看了一眼，谁也没说话。她伸手，从他肩膀上拈掉了一根松针。

就这么一下。

小满抬起头来。阿禾仍旧脚尖抵着树根，脖子伸着，一本正经地道：「你欠我的鸡蛋，现在是三个。」

小满便把昨儿夜里在山洞里算的那笔账，原原本本地算给她听：「本来欠你半个——芦花鸡没下的那一个。昨儿早上又借了一个，利息是两个，这就是两个半。可那个鸡蛋，我没吃，我转手给了……」说到这里，他顿了一顿，隔着衣裳按了按胸口，「……给了一个比我还饿的。转借是要加利的，所以是三个。再加上本来那半个，是三个半。」

阿禾张着嘴，好半天没合上。村口的人又笑了，这一回笑的却是阿禾。她大约是做梦也没想到，这世上竟有人自己往自己的账上加利息。她想了一想，拿指头点了点自己的脑门，道：「……三个半。记在这儿了。」顿了一顿，又道：「那个比你还饿的，是谁？」

小满道：「一只狐狸。」

阿禾盯着他看了半天，大约是在掂量这话里有几分真，最后道：「那它也得还。」

小满他爹站在鹿旁边，当着全村人的面，把这头鹿分了一遍。分得跟前一日晌午在山涧边上一模一样，一个字都不差：「鹿皮，交马家的租。肉，给他娘换一身新棉袄。给吴婆婆，送一条腿。」说到这里，他转过身来，冲着老周一拱手，「再给你家，赔一颗白菜。」

那天夜里，小满照旧把胸口那团东西揣在怀里睡。它一整天都没醒，身子一直是凉的，他拿两只手捂着它，捂了半夜，也没捂热。他睁着眼睛，听着它很慢、很慢地喘气，一口，又一口，每一口中间，都隔得那么长，长得他每一回都要屏住了气等。等着等着，便想起来，今天他有两回想跟它说一句话，两回都没说成。

一回是在崖上，它叫他先应他爹。

一回是在溪边，它掉下来了。

他对着黑暗，在心里把那句话又说了一遍，说得清清楚楚，一个字也没漏。可在心里说的，不算。
story.en:
Her voice was very soft, very tired, as if drifting from very, very far away. Xiaoman shifted half an inch to the left.

The reeds not yet straight. His fingers let go.

The arrow was gone off the string with a *whoosh*; before he'd seen where it flew, he felt his shoulder go light. The little silver fox slid off his neck, limp, falling. He dropped the bow and caught it — its eyes shut, its body cold as ice, more frightening even than last night's fever. Last night it had been hot, and hot at least meant alive; now it was cold, cold as a stone in the stream. Xiaoman panicked, stuffed it inside his clothes and held it against his chest, and through his patched-on-patched shirt felt it, very, very slowly, still breathing.

He opened his mouth. He meant to say "Thanks," or "Thank you," or something — some sentence with *thanks* in it. The words had reached the tip of his tongue, but its eyes were shut, and it couldn't hear.

By the stream the stag crashed down. The arrow was in its neck, dead centre.

His father limped over at a run — that leg that a moment ago couldn't stand now found strength from somewhere and ran faster than Old Zhou. He dropped to his knees beside the deer — never mind the knee — reached for the antlers and stroked them, once, twice, then turned to look at his son and smiled like a child.

Xiaoman smiled too. But his hand stayed pressed to his chest, not daring to let go.

Old Zhou ran down to the stream, looked at the deer, then the arrow, then Xiaoman, and smacked his lips. "One arrow?" Xiaoman's father said, "One arrow." "He shot it?" "He shot it." "He's only twelve." "Mm." Old Zhou looked at him a long while. "At twelve, you'd never touched that bow." His father said, "I was fourteen. My father was fourteen too." He paused, bent his head, stroking the deer's neck again and again with his palm, and said: "He's twelve."

He said nothing else. But the tone he said those three words in was not the tone he used to say "Third Master" to Ma San.

By the time they reached the village gate it was evening.

Under the old locust tree stood Xiaoman's mother, both hands tucked in her sleeves, motionless, as though she'd been standing a long time. Later Xiaoman learned she'd stood there from dark the day before to dusk this day — a whole night, a whole day — going home only once, to put a handful of wood on the stove: if they came back, she said, the stove couldn't be cold.

Beside her stood Ahe, and stood very oddly: the toes of both feet pressed exactly against the root of the old locust, not moving out an inch, while her body leaned forward, far forward, neck stretched like a goose waiting to be fed. At first Xiaoman didn't understand why she stood like that; then he remembered — her mother wouldn't let her past the village gate, and the old locust was the village gate. Not one foot of her had gone out; her neck, though, had.

His mother didn't shout. She walked over from under the old locust, neither fast nor slow, came up to her son, and stopped. First she looked at his face a while; then at his hands a while; last at his swollen left wrist. Round the wrist was the half strip of hem left over from wiping the fox's wounds last night, wound on anyhow, soaked by mud into a rotten rag.

Without a word his mother unwound the rag, tore a clean strip from under her own jacket, and wrapped it round again, turn by turn. She wrapped very slowly, very carefully, one turn, a tug, another turn, and at the end tied a knot — a knot square and neat, exactly like the ones she tied mending clothes. When she'd done, her hand rested on his wrist a moment.

Then she turned to look at Xiaoman's father. He was carrying the back of the door-plank, his face still unwashed of mud, his eyes red as a rabbit's. The two of them looked at each other, and neither spoke. She reached out and picked a pine needle off his shoulder.

Just that.

Ahe, toes still against the root, neck still stretched, said, perfectly serious: "The eggs you owe me — it's three now."

So Xiaoman laid out for her the whole sum he'd worked in the cave last night: "I owed you half to start with — the one the speckled hen didn't lay. Yesterday morning I borrowed one more, interest two, that's two and a half. But I didn't eat that egg; I passed it on to…" here he paused, and pressed his chest through his clothes, "…to someone hungrier than me. Passing a loan on adds interest, so that's three. Plus the half from before — three and a half."

Ahe stood open-mouthed for ages. The villagers laughed again, and this time it was Ahe they laughed at; she'd never have dreamed there was anyone in the world who'd add interest to his own debt. She thought, tapped her forehead with a finger. "…Three and a half. It's in here." A pause. "The one hungrier than you — who was it?"

Xiaoman said, "A fox."

Ahe stared at him a long while, weighing how much of it was true, and finally said: "Then it owes me too."

That evening Xiaoman's father, beside the deer, in front of the whole village, divided it up — exactly as at the stream the day before, not a word different: "The hide, for the Mas' rent. The meat, a new padded coat for his mother. A leg for Granny Wu." Here he turned and bowed to Old Zhou. "And for your family, a cabbage made good."

That night Xiaoman slept with the thing on his chest held inside his jacket as before. It hadn't woken all day; its body stayed cold; he cupped it in both hands half the night and couldn't warm it. He lay with his eyes open, listening to it breathe, very, very slowly, one breath, then another, each so far from the last that every time he held his own breath to wait. Waiting, he remembered that twice today he'd meant to say something to it, and twice he hadn't.

Once on the cliff, when it told him to answer his father first.

Once by the stream, when it fell.

Into the dark, in his heart, he said the thing again, clearly, not a word left out. But said in your heart doesn't count.

exits.means: ignores the wind and shoots straight

story.zh:
小满没理那句话。风？风懂什么。他照直放了箭。

箭擦着鹿角飞了过去，「笃」地钉进了溪对岸的泥里，尾羽还在晃。那头雄鹿猛地抬起头来，往四下里看了看，没看见人，只看见一支插在泥里、还在摇头晃脑的箭。它喷了一口白气，倒像在笑话这支箭，又低下头去，接着喝水。

他爹没说话，从箭壶里抽出第二支箭，递了过来。他肩上那团银毛，很轻很轻地，哼了一声。
story.en:
Xiaoman ignored it. Wind? What does the wind know. He loosed straight.

The arrow grazed the antlers and stuck *thock* in the mud across the stream, fletching still quivering. The stag's head came up; it looked all round, saw no one, only an arrow standing in the mud, still wagging its head. It snorted a white breath, as though laughing at the arrow, and lowered its head to drink again.

His father said nothing; he drew a second arrow from the quiver and handed it over. The silver fur on his shoulder gave a very, very small *hmph*.
